text:
From Sunsets to Sidelines: Events to Kick Off September

Well, friends, August is officially saying goodbye—and September is sliding in as if it owns the place. But around here, we don’t exactly close the door on summer just because the calendar says it’s time. This week along the Alabama Gulf Coast, you can still catch a sunset from the water on local cruises, shop local (ALWAYS), get your creative juices flowing, groove to free live outdoor music, hop aboard a train and visit a historic one, lace up for a football-loving 5K, and finish the week with a Labor Day celebration complete with laser lights, a visit from Tink and fireworks. So whether you’re squeezing out one more bit of summer fun or already mentally decorating for the holidays (yes, really), there’s plenty happening from the shores, the shine, and beyond. Let’s get into what’s up and what’s good on the coast this week!

Monday, August 31st- Experience the last day of August in style with a sunset Dolphin Cruise aboard the Fun Boats in Orange Beach. The sun is still shining, the air remains warm, and not surprisingly, our local wild dolphins are still making appearances throughout our beautiful salty waters. The boat sets sail for a delightful two-hour cruise, offering more than just a scenic water view. It’s also a wonderful chance to enjoy an educational marine life experience, where the crew dishes out facts and more, plus you might even participate in a water war with the company's second boat, and last but not least, witness a breathtaking Gulf Coast sunset—something that us locals never tire of. Tickets for all ages, including infants, are just $30 plus tax. Book now through the link below for an exciting adventure where dolphins are guaranteed to appear, and unforgettable memories are sure to be made.

Sunset Dolphin Cruise with the Fun Boats

Tuesday, September 1st- The Coastal Alabama Farmers and Fisherman’s Market is open every Saturday from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m., year-round, with fresh seafood, locally produced artisanal goods, choice meats, crafts, and other handmade items. Throughout the year, they also host exciting pop-up markets for special occasions and events. This Tuesday, kick off September with a visit to explore the Market with a unique Thanksgiving and Christmas twist—supplies for planters, magnolia reefs, garlands, and custom designs. Though September has just begun, it’s never too early to start preparing for the upcoming holidays. This vibrant market is hosted by The FlorAL Market, where designers will be on-site to help you choose the right supplies and share how-tos for creating your perfect holiday decor! Happy shopping, planning, and designing. For more info, please call Meredith at 251-200-1429.

Tuesday Market- Foley

Wednesday, September 2nd- The Gulf Shores Public Library is excited to offer a fun, engaging Homeschool Discovery series twice a month from September through December. These sessions feature hands-on learning activities that are educational and enjoyable for local kids and visitors alike. Join us this Wednesday to jump-start this new program, which this week will include creative writing techniques, frameworks, and helpful tips on the writing process. An instructor will guide the group through these skills, and writing prompts will be tailored to different grade levels so every student can participate and succeed. The program begins at 10:30 AM. Additionally, on the first Wednesday of each month at 4 PM, the library will host special programs for tweens and teens. They can choose to participate in a Nintendo Switch tournament, where they can showcase their racing skills in a bracket-style competition against up to three players on their own devices—space is limited, so please plan accordingly. The other option is their Pokémon Club, also starting at 4 PM, where participants can bring their cards to trade, share, and join fun activities and discussions about their favorite Pokémon. It's a great chance to make new friends! Remember, you can bring your own cards or games, but don't worry if you don't have any—library loaner decks are available. Come and enjoy all that the Gulf Shores Public Library has to offer—sign up, register, or learn more about these events with the link below.

Homeschool Discovery & Tween and Teen programs-GS

Thursday, September 3rd- The Sunset series at Gulf Place returns this fall in Gulf Shores. Join the community and their guests on the Town Green for free concerts—yes, live music outdoors, overlooking the beautiful white-sand shores at sunset. They’ve expanded the event to include an interactive selection of community experiences that will create even more engaging atmospheres for residents and visitors alike. Let’s break it down: alongside enjoying free live music, attendees will have opportunities to connect with local businesses, organizations, and non-profits that will be set up, as well as community partners. Break the ice with activities, demonstrations, educational displays, and, best of all, giveaways. Come along to mingle and enjoy these interactive experiences. This Thursday marks the beginning of the musical lineup with Chubby Carrier and the Bayou Swamp Band. The fun starts at 5 PM. The DJ will play until six, with the live concert beginning at 6 PM and running through to 8 PM. Come hungry and plan to enjoy your dinner from this week‘s food truck, Beachin’ Eats, and treat yourself after with Kona Ice. The Coastal Alabama Business Chamber will also be on-site at each concert selling beverages suitable for all ages. Here are some of the vendors participating this week: the Alabama Coastal Foundation with Share the Beach, Blue Girl Studio, Gulf Coast Eco Center, Bon Secour National Wildlife Refuge, the Gulf Shores City Store, and the Gulf Shores Police Department. You don’t want to miss out on this fall’s sunset series and its expansion. We’ll see you there.

Sunset Series Live FREE music- GS

Friday, September 4th- Take it easy while still enjoying an exciting time this Friday in downtown Foley. Bring the kids and enjoy a thrilling train ride at Heritage Park, then hop off and find a quaint spot in the park for an outdoor picnic. Don’t miss the historic train museum filled with fascinating exhibits. Families can snap unforgettable photos with the vintage locomotive and explore lovely pastimes just outside. Treat yourself to a visit to Stacey‘s Old-Time Soda Fountain for a sweet delight or stop by Yaba's sweet shop for a variety of tasty treats and lunch if you didn’t bring that picnic with you, both nearby and walking distance. Immerse yourself in the sights, sounds, and rich history of downtown Foley this Friday for a day full of fun and adventure, toot toot!

Railroad Museum and more-Foley

Saturday, September 5th- Get ready to lace up and kick off Labor Day weekend with a bit of exercise and lots of spirit for this year's annual Bloody Mary 5K run and walk at Tacky Jacks. Join others for the 11th annual race in Gulf Shores, where runners or walkers arrive at 6 AM on a flat, no-hill course, allowing you to enjoy at your own pace and any skill level a beautiful morning along Alabama’s beaches. This race marks the final event in the Run the Coast Summer Series for 2026. If you’re unfamiliar with the series, it’s for runners who want to test themselves and compete for prizes—not just any prizes, but cash awards given to the top three male and female finishers. These are based on their overall points across all three races. Don’t worry if you haven’t participated before; you can still join in and enjoy this 5K run or walk and reward yourself with a drink at the finish line back at Tacky Jacks Waterway Village, win spirit awards and medals for top age groups. Since football season has officially begun, many participants also use this race as a tradition to show off their favorite team colors. Whether you wear your running gear or your team's jersey or T-shirt, be ready to stand up and out and cheer for your football team. Happy running and team spirit repping!

11th Annual Bloody Mary 5K-GS

Sunday, September 6th- Come and light up Labor Day in Orange Beach this Sunday from 6 to 9 PM, or arrive an hour earlier for live music at Portside starting at 5 PM. At the Wharf, there’s always a party or something exciting to enjoy. From 6 to 9 PM, enjoy a DJ on Main Street, where traffic will be closed so children and families can run up and down the street and visit shops, illuminated by the light-up palm trees, with dancing and anticipation for the 8:45 PM Firework Bonanza. Fifteen minutes before the fireworks, the renowned SPECTRA laser light experience begins and will run again at 9 PM and 9:30 PM. There will be plenty of games to keep the children entertained, camel rides, and a very special guest appearance from Tinker Bell. Admission to this event is free, as is parking. Families can eat before they arrive or choose from a variety of sit-down and take-away restaurants, ranging from pizza to a steak at Villagio. There’s no wrong way to enjoy light-up Labor Day this Sunday at The Wharf. Who’s coming?

Light Up Labor Day

August may be clocking out, but the coast is still popping! So snag your friends, pick your fun, and send summer off on a high note. See ya’ll out there!

text:
Secularism does not free the human race. It leaves the species with only one project: take the earth (and now space) and call the taking progress.
A people that will not answer to a good above appetite becomes a gang with better tools. It maps the planet, writes procedures for the spoils, and congratulates itself on having no king but desire. The small raider is named a criminal. The large one is named a state, a market, a “values-neutral” order. The work is the same. Only the navy has grown.
Without a justice that judges the strong, law is a compact for dividing what was seized. Education becomes recruitment. Rights become weapons. Compassion becomes a story told after the raid. The child, the neighbor, and the dead are managed as inventory. That is not adulthood. That is infestation with good branding.
Christendom is the refusal of that lie. It tells man he is not the highest thing in the room. The neighbor is not plunder. The vow is not a deal. The table is not a split of loot. There is a King whose realm is not a takeover. Drop that, and humanity is only the cleverest pack that ever won a world. Keep it, and the species is offered a greater good than victory: a life that is not theft, even when it rules.

text:
Xi kicks off state visit to Kyrgyzstan, hailing "golden period" of cooperation

Chinese President Xi Jinping landed in Bishkek on Sunday for a state visit to Kyrgyzstan and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit 2026.

The China-Kyrgyzstan cooperation has ushered in a "golden period" of rapid development, Xi said in a written speech delivered upon his arrival.

TIME-HONORED FRIENDSHIP

Noting that China and Kyrgyzstan share a time-honored traditional friendship, Xi said that the majestic Tianshan Mountains stand as witnesses to the millennia of friendly exchanges between their peoples.

Over the 34 years since the establishment of diplomatic relations, the China-Kyrgyzstan relationship has withstood the test of a changing international landscape, maintained sound and stable development throughout, and reached the high level of a comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era, Xi said.

In recent years, bilateral trade volume and people-to-people exchanges have reached new highs, Xi said, noting that major projects including the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway have been successfully implemented, and the tangible results of mutually beneficial cooperation have broadly benefited the two peoples.

Xi said that during the visit he will have in-depth exchanges of views with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov on China-Kyrgyzstan relations, cooperation in various fields between the two countries, and international and regional issues of common concern, and draw a new blueprint for building a China-Kyrgyzstan community with a shared future.

"I look forward to attending the SCO Bishkek Summit, working with all parties to revisit the 25-year development experience of the SCO, jointly discuss cooperation plans, create the future of the organization, and promote the continuous new development of the SCO," Xi said.

HIGH-QUALITY DEVELOPMENT OF TIES

Ahead of his state visit to Kyrgyzstan and attendance at the SCO summit, Xi on Friday published a signed article titled "Jointly Opening up New Prospects for the High-Quality Development of China-Kyrgyzstan Relations" in the Slovo Kyrgyzstana and the Kabar National News Agency.

Noting that it will be his third visit to this beautiful land, Xi said he looks forward to working with President Japarov to map out a new blueprint for China-Kyrgyzstan relations and make new progress in building an SCO community with a shared future.

Describing the two countries' relations as a "golden model" of good-neighborly friendship and mutually beneficial cooperation, Sheradil Baktygulov, director of the Kyrgyz Institute of World Politics in Bishkek, said high-level exchanges have provided clear strategic guidance for the deepening of bilateral relations and closer coordination between the two countries in international affairs.

In the signed article, Xi said that China and Kyrgyzstan are good neighbors sharing weal and woe, good partners with a shared future, and good friends who help each other succeed.

"When a neighboring country is genuinely happy about your success, that sincerity is truly precious. It reflects President Xi's respect for Kyrgyzstan, its people and the development path they have chosen," said former Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Alikbek Jekshenkulov. Noting the improved understanding between the two peoples, Jekshenkulov said such mutual understanding has kept bilateral friendship enduring and vibrant, allowing it to be passed down from generation to generation.

In February 2025, Xi and Japarov reached important common understandings on further deepening the comprehensive strategic partnership for the new era and building a China-Kyrgyzstan community with a shared future defined by good-neighborliness, friendship and shared prosperity. The decision opened a new chapter of bilateral relations.

In the signed article, Xi said China and Kyrgyzstan have complementary economies and immense cooperation potential. Despite sluggish global growth, the two countries' business cooperation has continued to make steady progress.

Tolonbek Abdyrov, professor of economics and vice rector of the International Higher School of Medicine in Kyrgyzstan, said the two countries enjoy enormous potential for cooperation. "Chinese investment has not only enabled Kyrgyzstan to implement a number of major infrastructure, energy and industrial projects, but has also created opportunities to accelerate the country's modernization."

Noting that Xi's signed article provides strong guidance for the sustainable development of bilateral cooperation, Kyrgyz economist Iskender Sharsheev said: "The two sides enjoy enormous potential for cooperation in such fields as the digital economy, green energy, and artificial intelligence."

In the article, Xi also called on the two sides to solidify good-neighborliness and friendship, pursue mutual benefit and win-win results, carry forward the traditional friendship, and practice multilateralism.

Xi said China is ready to work with Kyrgyzstan to steadily advance their multifaceted cooperation, channel the streams of the two peoples' goodwill into the river of the two nations' friendship, and jointly open up new prospects for the high-quality development of China-Kyrgyzstan relations.

On the SCO summit, Xi said China is convinced that with the concerted efforts of all sides, this year's SCO summit will be a crowning success and provide fresh impetus for carrying forward the Shanghai Spirit and building an SCO community with a shared future.

Professor Almazbek Akmataliev, former rector of the Academy of Public Administration under the President of Kyrgyzstan, said in today's international environment, Xi's call for further carrying forward the Shanghai Spirit has become increasingly relevant.

HOPES FOR GREATER COOPERATION

People across Kyrgyzstan see Xi's visit as an important opportunity to deepen political trust, expand mutually beneficial cooperation, and boost people-to-people ties, which will inject new impetus into bilateral relations.

"We are witnessing one of the most meaningful and fruitful periods in the history of Kyrgyz-Chinese relations," said Jekshenkulov. Xi's visit will represent not only another milestone, but also an opportunity to elevate bilateral ties to a new level, he said.

Kanaiym Baktygulova, former Kyrgyz ambassador to China, has witnessed the development of bilateral ties at close range. She said the political wisdom and strategic vision of the two leaders have provided a solid foundation for the growth of bilateral relations and charted a clear course for future cooperation.

Baktygulova said she expected Xi to put forward new proposals for deepening mutual political trust and expanding win-win cooperation.

Noting that Kyrgyzstan is implementing its National Development Program until 2030 and China is advancing the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), Elkinbek Ashirbaev, governor of Kyrgyzstan's Chui region, voiced his hope that Xi's visit will help bring the two countries' development strategies into closer alignment.

For Kyrgyz economist Abdyrov, China's experience in infrastructure, industrial modernization and the clean energy industry is particularly relevant to his country's development needs.

Abdyrov also sees useful lessons in China's approach to long-term development. Strategic planning and consistent industrial policies can offer insights into Kyrgyzstan's pursuit of sustainable growth, he said, adding that the visit could encourage further exchanges on governance.

In recent years, people-to-people and cultural exchanges between China and Kyrgyzstan have continued to deepen and yield tangible results. Zhyldyz Bakashova, director of the State Book Chamber, said she expects Xi's visit to promote further cooperation in book publishing and translation, helping readers in both countries better understand each other's cultures.

The two countries are also working together to study and protect cultural heritage through the China-Kyrgyzstan Belt and Road Joint Laboratory on Cultural Heritage Conservation.

"By studying and protecting cultural heritage together, we have gained a deeper understanding of the histories of both countries," said Aisin Duishanalieva, the laboratory's Kyrgyz director, expecting the leaders' meeting to offer further support to that collaboration.

At a time of heightened global uncertainty, Kyrgyz-China collaboration in the United Nations, the SCO and other multilateral forums has become increasingly valuable, said Baktygulov, highlighting China's support for Kyrgyzstan's successful election in June as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council.

Baktygulov said he expects the visit to strengthen bilateral communication and coordination on regional and global affairs, and promote joint efforts to maintain regional stability, enhance dialogue and seek solutions to hotspot issues. (via Xinhua News)

Mystery Book Clubs That Keep Everyone Guessing

A good mystery leaves a few tidbits under the log: a suspicious alibi, a detail that suddenly matters, and just enough doubt to make every reader feel clever. That is why mystery book clubs can create such lively gatherings. One person is certain the charming neighbor did it. Another is following the muddy paw prints. A third has suspected the victim since chapter two.

For readers who love small towns, memorable characters, and a mystery that does not require sleeping with the lights on, a book club can turn a quiet reading habit into a monthly treat. The secret is not picking the bloodiest crime or the buzziest title. It is choosing stories that give everyone something to talk about, then making room for friendly disagreement.

## What Makes Mystery Book Clubs So Much Fun?

Mystery readers are natural conversationalists. We notice clues, question motives, and form opinions before the detective has poured the second cup of coffee. A romance may invite a discussion about chemistry. A mystery invites a discussion about practically everyone.

The genre also suits a wide range of readers. Cozy mysteries offer humor, community, pets, food, and clever crimes without graphic violence. Traditional mysteries often bring atmosphere and puzzle-solving to the foreground. Historical mysteries let a group visit another time and place, while animal-centered mysteries add an observant companion with a nose for trouble. The best choice depends on what your members enjoy, but a shared love of asking, “Did you see that coming?” goes a long way.

Mysteries are especially generous to groups with mixed reading speeds. Someone who finished last night can share a favorite clue. Someone who read more slowly can still join the conversation about the setting, the characters, or which suspect gave them the oddest feeling. Just agree in advance whether the discussion will include spoilers. Nothing silences a room faster than revealing the culprit before everyone has met the victim.

## Start With the Right Kind of Mystery

Before choosing a first book, decide what feeling you want members to take home. A club built around cozy mysteries should feel welcoming, witty, and a little curious, much like gathering around a kitchen table while rain taps the window. A darker crime-fiction club may prefer moral dilemmas, tense pacing, and cases that linger after the final page.

There is no wrong answer, but clarity prevents disappointment. A reader looking for warm small-town charm may not enjoy a grim serial-killer novel, even if it is beautifully written. Likewise, readers who want intricate police procedure may be impatient with a mystery where a clever baker, librarian, veterinarian, or dog helps solve the case.

A useful first pick has a satisfying solution, a manageable length, and enough suspects to inspire debate. It should also stand alone or work well as the opening of a series. Series mysteries are particularly friendly for book clubs because returning characters become familiar neighbors. Members begin to care not only about who committed the crime, but also whether the protagonist will finally repair that old house, trust a new friend, or keep a curious pet out of the evidence locker.

For a cozy, animal-loving group, the Doc and Daisy Mysteries offer a playful example of this blend: a Florida setting, canine forensics, and Daisy the dog sharing her observations with a warm snout and a sharp eye for human nonsense.

https://t.co/YiqiG7h8vF

### Rotate Subgenres Without Losing the Club’s Personality

Variety keeps a club fresh, especially after several meetings. One month might feature a village mystery with a historic landmark. The next could be a locked-room puzzle, a holiday whodunit, or a mystery told through the perspective of an animal companion. A seasonal choice can be fun, too: beach-town intrigue in summer, a harvest festival mystery in fall, or a snowed-in inn when winter arrives.

Still, do not rotate so wildly that members cannot tell what kind of club they joined. If your group loves cozy stories, keep the warmth and lower violence level as a general rule. If you occasionally choose something outside that comfort zone, mention it clearly when you announce the title. A little warning is kinder than a surprise corpse in chapter one.

## Make the Discussion Feel Like Sleuthing

The best mystery book club questions do more than ask whether members liked the book. They invite readers to retrace the investigation and examine their own assumptions. Start by asking when everyone formed a theory. Then ask what clue changed their minds, or what clue they missed entirely.

Talk about the detective’s methods. Did the amateur sleuth act wisely, or did they wander into danger because the plot needed them to? Was the official investigator helpful, skeptical, or suspiciously absent? In cozy mysteries, it can also be fun to discuss why the community allows one person to stumble across so many crimes without moving away immediately.

Characters offer another rich trail. Ask which suspect seemed most believable, which relationship felt true to life, and whether the victim was more complicated than first expected. A thoughtful mystery does not always make the culprit a monster. Sometimes it shows how jealousy, fear, greed, or old hurt can lead an ordinary person in a terrible direction.

Setting deserves its own attention. Small towns, coastal communities, bookstores, veterinary clinics, gardens, and historic homes can do more than provide a pretty backdrop. They shape who knows whom, where secrets can hide, and which local traditions become useful clues. Readers often enjoy comparing the setting they imagined with the one other members saw in their minds.

If your club includes animal lovers, ask what the pets add to the story. Are they comic relief, emotional anchors, accidental clue-finders, or wiser than the humans around them? A dog may not testify in court, but a determined nose can point a story in an interesting direction.

## Keep Meetings Easy and Welcoming

A mystery book club does not need elaborate rules. A regular day, a comfortable place to meet, and a way to share the next title are enough. Some groups meet at a library, coffee shop, bookstore, community room, or a member’s home. Others gather by video call, which can be a lovely option for readers who live far apart or prefer to bring their own blanket and cat.

If food is part of the fun, let it nod to the book without turning the host into a short-order cook. Tea and cookies suit almost any cozy mystery. A Florida-set story might inspire citrus treats. A bakery mystery practically asks for something sweet. Keep it optional, though. The conversation matters more than a perfectly themed snack table.

A simple meeting rhythm helps quieter members enter the conversation. Begin with a spoiler-free first impression for anyone still deciding whether to read the book. Then move into full discussion, theories, favorite scenes, and the ending. Near the close, choose the next selection or offer two or three options for a vote. Giving members a little say builds commitment without making every choice a committee hearing.

## Let the Group Be More Than a Reading Assignment

The strongest clubs create a small tradition around curiosity and kindness. Celebrate a member’s birthday, welcome a new reader, or spend a few minutes sharing other mysteries people have enjoyed recently. If someone disliked the book, that is not a problem. A respectful disagreement can be the most entertaining part of the evening.

It also helps to remember that not every reader experiences a mystery the same way. Some solve the case early and enjoy watching the clues fall into place. Others avoid guessing because they prefer the surprise. Some read for the puzzle, while others are there for the friendships, the setting, and the lovable dog asleep beside the detective’s desk. A good club leaves room for all of them.

The next time your group gathers, do not worry about finding the perfect question or predicting every twist. Put the kettle on, open the book, and let one suspicious detail start the conversation. Somewhere between the alibis, the laughter, and the last cookie, your readers may find exactly what a good mystery promises: a reason to look closer.

The intellectual class loves a contradiction, provided it allows them to keep their hands in the cookie jar. In *The Road to Serfdom*, Friedrich Hayek nails the fundamental delusion of the modern progressive: the idea that you can build a centralized, planned engine of control while simultaneously pretending to safeguard individual liberty. It’s a performance of virtue designed to mask a grab for power.

They love to offer these hollow "declarations of rights" that look good on a poster, but they always include a backdoor. As Hayek points out, even a proponent like H.G. Wells tries to grant the right to trade, only to immediately render it "nugatory" by qualifying it with the vague requirement that actions be "compatible with the common welfare."

That’s the ultimate linguistic trap. Because the planners define the "common welfare" to suit their own ends, the "right" becomes a ghost. You aren't being granted a liberty; you're being granted a permission slip that the state can shred the moment it becomes inconvenient. It’s not a dilemma to these intellectuals—it's a feature. They want the moral high ground of the "rights of man" and the absolute authority of the planner, and they think they can have both through sheer semantic gymnastics. 🦫

text:
HE TOLD GRADUATES TO WORK A HUNDRED HOURS. THAT SAME YEAR HE TOLD HIS OWN COMPANY SOMETHING ELSE.

@elonmusk 

On May 16, 2014, the USC Marshall School of Business gave its undergraduate commencement address to a man who said he had about six minutes and would try to say the most useful things he could think of.

He offered four rules. The first was to work.

Not work well. Work hard, and he was specific about what hard meant. When he and his brother started their first company they rented an office instead of an apartment and slept on the couch. They showered at the YMCA. They had one computer between them, so the website ran during the day and he wrote code at night, seven days a week.

Then he gave the graduates a number, and the number is the whole reason this post exists. If someone else is working fifty hours and you are working a hundred, you will get twice as much done.

That speech is on the USC channel, free, and he is on camera saying it.

Four years later, in November 2018, he compressed the same idea into nine words on Twitter: nobody ever changed the world on 40 hours a week.

So the position is not ambiguous. It is the loudest public argument on Earth for one variable, and the variable is time.

But the part worth writing down isn't the speech. It's what he sent his own employees seven months before that tweet.

On April 17, 2018, Tesla staff received an internal email about production. Attached to the end of it were six productivity recommendations. Electrek and Jalopnik obtained the email that day, and CNBC confirmed it was real.

Read the six and count how many are about working longer.

Get rid of large meetings unless they clearly serve everyone in the room, and if they do, keep them short. Get rid of frequent meetings unless something is genuinely urgent, and cut the frequency the moment it stops being urgent. Leave a meeting, or drop off a call, the second it is obvious you are not adding anything — in his words, it is not rude to leave, it is rude to make someone stay. Stop using acronyms and internal jargon, because anything that needs explaining slows communication down. Let information travel by the shortest route that gets the job done rather than up and down a chain of command. And when a rule stops making sense, treat that as a problem with the rule.

The count is zero.

Not one of the six mentions hours, effort, weekends, or sleeping at the office. Every single one is about removing interruption and communication overhead from a working day.

Here is your ten seconds of arithmetic, and it is his own.

His claim to the graduates was that a hundred hours produces twice what fifty produces. That claim only holds if an hour of work is a fixed unit — if hour number ninety-nine contains the same amount of thinking as hour number four, and if an hour interrupted six times is worth the same as an hour that isn't.

His email is a six-point statement that this is false. You do not write rules banning meetings and jargon and chains of command if the hour is a fixed unit. You write them because the hour is being eaten from the inside, and you have decided that what it is being eaten by is worth attacking directly.

One document sells the first variable. The other document, sent to the people who actually have to produce, quietly protects the second.

Now put a price on the thing his email attacks.

Gloria Mark, Chancellor's Professor of Informatics at UC Irvine, has spent two decades measuring exactly this. Not surveying people — following them around offices with a stopwatch and timing every event to the second. In her 2018 talk at Google she put the finding on a single slide: the median focus duration on any computer screen is 40 seconds.

Forty seconds. Then something else.

An eight-hour day is 28,800 seconds. At that median, you are looking at roughly seven hundred switches between one morning and one evening.

That is what Musk's six rules are aimed at. Not laziness. Not insufficient commitment. The rate.

And it explains why the two documents can both be sincere and still contradict each other. Adding hours to a day that fragments seven hundred times does not add proportional output. It adds fragmented hours. The man who told a stadium that a hundred hours beats fifty was, four years later, writing to his own engineers about the only thing that determines what an hour is worth.

Which produces the actual rule here, and it is not work more.

If the hour is fixed, buy more hours. If the hour is not fixed, the hours you already have are the cheapest thing you will ever fix, and every one you add before fixing them arrives pre-broken.

Both of these documents are public. One is a commencement speech with millions of views, quoted in every hustle thread ever written. The other is an internal email that leaked, and it is the one he wrote when the audience was people who had to actually ship a car.

text:
When Serbs Do Their Part, Why Do the Rules Change?

I think there is a very clear pattern in the agreements Serbs have made with Western governments and international institutions over the last 30 years.

The problem is not only that agreements were later broken or only partially implemented. The bigger problem is that the words themselves seem to change meaning once the Serbian side has already implemented its obligations.

The Dayton Agreement, UNSC Resolution 1244 and the 2013 Brussels Agreement are very different instruments, negotiated at different times and under different circumstances. That makes the pattern even more striking: despite all those differences, the same problem keeps appearing.

Once forces have withdrawn, institutions have been integrated or competencies have been transferred, those steps become facts on the ground. But what was promised in return can still be reinterpreted, delayed or debated for years.

1. The Dayton Peace Agreement

Republic of Srpska accepted the constitutional order agreed in the DPA in 1995. Annex 10 describes the High Representative and lists his functions: monitoring implementation, maintaining contact with the parties, coordinating civilian organizations, helping resolve difficulties and reporting on implementation.

It says nothing about making laws, removing elected officials or overruling parliaments.

After Dayton, the Peace Implementation Council, or PIC, was created to coordinate international support for implementation. It was not created by Annex 10, is not mentioned in Annex 10, and the parties to Dayton never granted it any power there to expand the authority of the High Representative. 

Yet it later became the framework through which the so-called Bonn Powers were developed, expanding the High Representative far beyond the functions actually written into the agreement.

Without our consent, the office evolved into something much closer to a colonial governor, able to impose laws and remove elected officials in a country still subject to extraordinary foreign supervision more than 30 years after Dayton. And once those powers existed, they were repeatedly used to reshape the institutional balance created at Dayton. Many of the most consequential interventions reduced Republic of Srpska’s competencies while strengthening institutions at the Bosnia and Herzegovina level.

Yes, the High Representative is the final authority regarding interpretation. But the power to interpret an agreement is not the power to rewrite it. If such extraordinary powers were intended, they could have been written into Annex 10 in 1995. They weren't.

The appointment issue follows the same pattern. Annex 10 speaks about a High Representative being appointed consistent with relevant UN Security Council resolutions.

Christian Schmidt never received a UN Security Council resolution endorsing his designation. The PIC had already designated him when, in 2021, the Security Council considered a resolution that would have expressly welcomed and agreed to that designation. It was not adopted.

Schmidt nevertheless took office claiming both the authority of High Representative and the additional Bonn Powers developed through that same PIC.

And that brings the two issues together. Serbs agreed to Annex 10. We did not agree that a body absent from the agreement could expand the powers of the High Representative and then decide who gets to exercise those expanded powers.

Serbs signed the words written in the agreement. We did not sign some imaginary "spirit of Dayton" that only foreign diplomats apparently understand and can redefine whenever the actual words become inconvenient.

2. UNSC Resolution 1244

Yugoslavia withdrew its army and police from Kosovo. Nobody had any difficulty understanding what "withdraw" meant. Yugoslavia had to do something concrete and it did it.

But the same resolution speaks about sovereignty and territorial integrity, an interim international administration, substantial autonomy, a political process toward a settlement and the return of an agreed number of Yugoslav and Serbian personnel.

Then suddenly every one of those words becomes flexible.

"Interim" can apparently last for decades and end with major Western states recognizing Kosovo as independent.

"Sovereignty and territorial integrity" apparently do not prevent those same states from recognizing the separation of the territory.

A "settlement" apparently does not have to be a settlement accepted by Serbia.

And the agreed return of Yugoslav and Serbian personnel provided for in the resolution never took place.

Why did we accept that "withdraw" meant an immediate and complete withdrawal? By the same kind of creative interpretation used against Serbia later, "withdraw" could just as easily have been declared to mean withdrawing two personnel per year.

But Serbia didn't do that. Withdraw meant withdraw.

Only afterwards did we start hearing variations of the same explanations about the other words in Resolution 1244:

"1244 was status-neutral."

"It didn't prescribe the final outcome."

"The status quo was unsustainable."

"Kosovo is a unique, sui generis case."

"The declaration itself wasn't prohibited."

"The authors were acting outside the framework."

"Recognition is for individual states to decide."

And after enough of that, somehow "sovereignty and territorial integrity," "interim," "substantial autonomy" and "settlement" no longer seemed to carry anything close to the weight those words had when Yugoslavia withdrew its forces in 1999.

But nobody ever said:

"Well, perhaps 'withdraw' is subject to various interpretations." 

That word was apparently perfectly clear.

3. The 2013 Brussels Agreement

The Brussels Agreement may be the clearest example because the exchange is written almost side by side.

Major institutional changes were implemented on the ground. Serbian police structures in northern Kosovo were integrated into the Kosovo Police, members of other Serbian security structures were to be offered places in equivalent Kosovo structures, and judicial authorities were integrated into the Kosovo legal framework.

These were not vague promises about something that might happen one day. They were concrete institutional changes.

And what appears at the very beginning of the same agreement?

Point 1 says: "There will be an Association/Community of Serb majority municipalities in Kosovo."

And the following provisions are quite specific. The agreement says the Association/Community will be created by statute, will have its own structures and will exercise functions in areas including economic development, education, health and urban and rural planning.

That was signed in 2013. It is now 2026 and there is still no Association.

So once again, the agreed changes on the Serbian side became reality on the ground, while the central institutional commitment to the Serbian community remained unimplemented.

And notice the language again.

It does not say:

"The parties will consider whether an Association might perhaps be created in the future."

It says:

"There will be an Association/Community."

Apparently even "there will be" can become negotiable once Serbia has already implemented its part.

4. Reciprocity Has to Work Both Ways

These three cases are why I think Serbia and Republic of Srpska have to change not only how they negotiate agreements, but what happens when the other side fails to perform.

If the other side does not fulfill a fundamental part of an agreement, we cannot simply continue treating every step we implemented as permanent while asking politely for the other side to do the same.

If a fundamental obligation remains unfulfilled, measures implemented by the Serbian side that can still be reversed should not automatically be treated as permanent.

For Republic of Srpska, that means going back to the original Dayton arrangement that was actually signed and restoring competencies that were later taken or transferred under pressure, including through the exercise of the Bonn Powers, powers nowhere granted in the text of the Dayton Agreement.

For Kosovo, Serbia should treat all of Resolution 1244 as valid, not only the parts requiring Serbia to withdraw. The provisions concerning the agreed return of Yugoslav and Serbian personnel should finally be implemented.

And with Brussels, if there is still no Association after more than a decade, then Serbia should stop acting as if every institutional change it implemented under Brussels must remain permanent regardless of whether the other side ever implements its own commitments. Serbia should pursue the re-establishment of its institutions in accordance with the Serbian Constitution.

5. Agreements Need Consequences

Of course there would be political and economic pressure if Serbia started doing this. But there is also a price for never doing it.

If everybody knows that Serbia will fulfill its obligations, while the other side can delay, reinterpret or simply leave its own obligations unfulfilled for years without consequence, why should anyone respect the next agreement?

That creates exactly the wrong incentive. What the Serbian side implements becomes a permanent fact on the ground, while reciprocal obligations can remain open to interpretation or implementation for years.

That is the pattern that has to end.

The purpose is not escalation for its own sake. The purpose is to restore reciprocity and make non-performance carry a real cost.

The basic rule should be very simple:

The words in an agreement have to mean the same thing when they protect Serbs as they do when they bind Serbs.

text:
Russia’s Way of War: Terrible Beginnings, Overwhelming Conclusions

Russia frequently begins its wars looking incompetent.

Its commanders underestimate the enemy. Its troops arrive poorly supplied. Communications fail, vehicles break down and elaborate plans collapse almost immediately after meeting real resistance. Outside observers see the confusion and conclude that the Russian military has been exposed as a paper tiger.

Sometimes that conclusion is correct. Russia has lost wars, abandoned campaigns and suffered humiliating defeats.

But there is another pattern running through Russian military history—one far more dangerous than the initial incompetence suggests. When Russia survives the opening disaster, it can begin learning, copying, simplifying and mobilizing. What started as a clumsy expedition gradually becomes an industrial war of attrition.

The elegant original plan disappears. It is replaced by something cruder, larger and much harder to stop.

Russia often begins with a parade and discovers it is actually in a war. Then it starts building the army it should have brought in the first place.

That may be exactly what is happening with drones in Ukraine.

Russia is not brilliant at the beginning

Russian military history should not be reduced to a myth that Russia always wins in the end. It does not.

Imperial Russia was defeated by Japan in 1905. The Russian Empire collapsed during the First World War. The Soviet Union withdrew from Afghanistan after nearly a decade of fighting. Russia’s first war in Chechnya ended with Russian forces leaving after enormous losses and humiliation.

Failure is entirely possible.

But when Russia possesses enough territory, population, industrial capacity and political will to remain in a conflict, its most frightening advantage may be its ability to absorb a catastrophic opening without accepting that the war is over.

Russia is often less impressive as a finely tuned military machine than as a damaged machine that keeps rebuilding itself while still running.

Its strength is not avoiding mistakes. Its strength is surviving mistakes that would end the war for a less durable state.

Napoleon reached Moscow—but Russia reached Paris

Napoleon’s 1812 invasion initially appeared to confirm French superiority. Russian armies retreated. Napoleon advanced hundreds of miles into the Russian Empire and eventually occupied Moscow.

By the normal political logic of European warfare, taking one of an enemy’s most important cities should have forced a settlement. Instead, Russia refused to give Napoleon the ending he expected.

The Russian army traded territory for time. French supply lines stretched across enormous distances. Winter, hunger, disease, exhaustion and constant attacks reduced Napoleon’s army during its retreat.

Russia did not merely survive. Russian forces eventually carried the war westward. In 1814, they entered Paris.

The contrast was extraordinary: Moscow had been occupied in 1812, yet Russian troops stood in Napoleon’s capital less than two years later.

The lesson was not that Russian commanders had planned every stage perfectly. They had not. The lesson was that occupying Russian territory did not automatically destroy Russia’s capacity to continue the war.

Napoleon won the opening movement. Russia remained long enough to determine the conclusion.

In 1941, the Soviet Union looked finished

The most extreme example came in 1941.

Nazi Germany’s Operation Barbarossa shattered enormous Soviet formations. Millions of Soviet soldiers were killed, wounded or captured. Aircraft were destroyed on the ground. Command systems collapsed. German forces advanced to the outskirts of Moscow, occupied vast areas of Soviet territory and appeared close to destroying the Soviet state.

The Red Army’s performance was frequently disastrous. Stalin had purged experienced officers, ignored warnings and left his military unprepared. Soviet troops paid for those failures with suffering on an almost incomprehensible scale.

If the war had been judged by its first months, the Soviet Union should have disappeared.

It did not.

Factories were relocated east. New armies were raised. Equipment was simplified and manufactured in immense quantities. Soviet commanders learned how to coordinate armor, artillery, infantry, engineers and aircraft across fronts extending hundreds of miles.

The Soviet Union also received enormously valuable Allied assistance. American and British equipment, food, fuel, vehicles and raw materials helped keep Soviet forces moving. American Lend-Lease supplied approximately 400,000 vehicles, 14,000 aircraft, 13,000 tanks and millions of tons of food and petroleum products.[1]

Russia’s triumph was not accomplished alone, and it should never be romanticized. Soviet leadership consumed human lives with a brutality that few other governments could have politically survived.

But the military transformation was real.

In 1941, the Red Army was encircled and destroyed in formations containing hundreds of thousands of soldiers. By 1944, that same military system was conducting Operation Bagration, one of the largest and most successful offensives in military history, annihilating much of Germany’s Army Group Centre.[2]

In April 1945, approximately 2.5 million Soviet troops, supported by more than 6,000 tanks and over 40,000 artillery pieces, stood before Berlin.[3]

The military that had nearly collapsed outside Moscow finished the war in Hitler’s capital.

Terrible beginning. Overwhelming conclusion.

Chechnya provided another warning

Russia’s assault on Grozny in late 1994 was another demonstration of arrogance meeting reality.

Russian leaders expected an intimidating display of armor to overwhelm Chechen resistance. Instead, Russian columns entered an urban battlefield without adequate coordination, infantry protection or reliable communications. Chechen fighters attacked from buildings and side streets, destroying Russian vehicles throughout the city.

The performance exposed the decay of the post-Soviet armed forces.

Russia eventually withdrew from Chechnya under a 1996 agreement. That first war was a genuine Russian defeat.

But Moscow returned in 1999 with a different approach. Rather than sending armored columns directly into the same trap, Russia relied heavily upon artillery, airpower, siege tactics and overwhelming destructive force. Grozny was devastated. Russia then combined military operations with local political control and pro-Moscow Chechen forces.

The second campaign was not an example of graceful military genius. It was brutal adaptation.

Russia learned enough from its defeat to change the method, even if the replacement method depended upon destruction on a massive scale.

That is an important distinction in understanding Russia. Adaptation does not necessarily make Russian warfare cleaner, smarter or more humane.

It often makes it more systematic.

Ukraine began with another Russian disaster

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 followed the familiar opening pattern.

The Kremlin expected Ukraine’s government to collapse quickly. Russian units advanced with insufficient fuel, confused command relationships and inadequate logistical support. The long convoy north of Kyiv became the international symbol of the invasion: an army supposedly conducting a rapid conquest stalled along a roadway.

Russian airborne operations failed to deliver the decisive political collapse Moscow expected. Ukrainian forces attacked supply lines, destroyed armored vehicles and forced Russia to retreat from northern Ukraine.

The original campaign was a stunning failure.

Russia then narrowed its objectives, consolidated command structures and moved away from its unsuccessful attempt at rapid maneuver. It returned to methods it understood better: artillery, fortified defensive lines, attrition, mobilization, glide bombs and attacks against Ukrainian infrastructure.

U.S. Army analysis notes that Russia responded to its early failures by reducing its goals, reorganizing command and abandoning failed maneuver tactics in favor of a more attritional strategy.[4]

This did not transform Russia into an elegant military. Russian forces continued suffering enormous casualties. Corruption, poor leadership and logistical problems did not disappear.

But the expectation that the 2022 failure would automatically produce Russian collapse proved dangerously optimistic.

Russia remained in the war. And once it remained, it began changing.

The drone war shows the pattern happening again

Ukraine entered large-scale FPV warfare with an important innovative advantage. Ukrainian volunteers, engineers and military units adapted cheap commercial drones into precision weapons faster than Russia’s traditional defense system could respond.

For a time, Ukraine seemed to be inventing the future while Russia remained tied to artillery and massed assaults.

Russia then began doing what it has done in previous wars: observing what worked, copying it, simplifying it and increasing production.

By the end of 2024, the Russian military reportedly offered frontline units a catalog containing 58 types of FPV drones. Civilian manufacturers and volunteer organizations were producing as many as 40,000 FPVs per month, while Russian strike activity expanded from several hundred attacks to nearly 2,000 per day.[5]

Russia created specialized drone formations and established the Rubicon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies. Rubicon serves as a testing ground for new equipment and tactics, concentrating specialized drone units against valuable Ukrainian targets.

Russia also formalized unmanned-systems troops as a separate military branch.

That is the institutional shift we should be watching. Russia is no longer treating drones as temporary equipment purchased for one emergency. It is building them into the permanent structure of its armed forces.

Russia did not invent every weapon—it learned to use them

Russia’s Geran drone is based upon Iran’s Shahed design. Its early FPV tactics borrowed heavily from Ukrainian battlefield success. Many Russian drones still rely upon foreign electronics, including commercially available Western processors and components that continue reaching Russia despite sanctions.

None of that makes the resulting weapon less dangerous.

The Soviet Union also copied foreign technology, purchased equipment and incorporated Allied material. Russia’s historical talent has rarely depended upon inventing every important system first. It has depended upon identifying a useful design and determining how to manufacture and employ it at scale.

The Shahed is a perfect example.

Russia initially imported the Iranian weapon. It then signed an industrial agreement to manufacture modified Geran versions at the Alabuga facility in Tatarstan. Between January and September 2024, that facility reportedly produced 5,760 drones. Russia also mass-produced cheaper Gerbera decoys designed to resemble attacking drones on radar, forcing Ukraine to expend attention and air-defense ammunition determining which targets were real.[6]

That is adaptation through industrialization.

Russia did not need to invent the concept. It needed to turn it into a repeatable system of mass attack.

Fiber optics show Russia can innovate, too

Russia is not merely copying.

In March 2024, Russian forces reportedly became the first side in the war to introduce fiber-optic-controlled FPV drones operationally.[7] These drones unspool a thin physical cable while flying, maintaining their connection with the operator even inside areas protected by powerful electronic jamming.

The solution sounds almost old-fashioned. Instead of creating a more advanced radio, Russia bypassed the radio problem entirely.

Fiber-optic drones reportedly became particularly important during fighting in the Kursk region. They could enter heavily jammed areas where conventional FPVs lost their signals. Ukraine subsequently developed its own versions, continuing the rapid cycle in which each side copies and counters the other.

That is what real wartime innovation looks like. It does not always emerge from a billion-dollar laboratory. Sometimes it comes from solving one immediate battlefield problem with the simplest available answer.

The V2U may represent the next threshold

Russia’s V2U drone is more disturbing because it appears to move beyond remote piloting.

Examination of recovered systems reportedly found powerful onboard computers, cameras and the processing capacity needed for computer vision. The apparent absence of standard communications equipment led analysts to conclude that at least some V2U versions may navigate, search for targets and attack without a continuous connection to a human operator.

A 2026 study from the Center for Strategic and International Studies concluded that Russia has likely fielded a fully autonomous unmanned system in combat. The report described evidence consistent with independent navigation, target selection and possible coordination between drones.[8]

This does not mean Russia has created a science-fiction intelligence that understands the battlefield as a human does. The system may only identify objects matching limited categories—a vehicle, road target or visual pattern.

That is still an extraordinary change.

An autonomous drone does not require a radio link that can be jammed. It does not require an operator to remain connected during the final approach. It can potentially be assigned an area rather than one precisely designated target.

The weapon is no longer merely a flying bomb.

It is becoming a hunter.

The attack on the market vendor was probably human-controlled

The recent video showing a Russian drone pursuing a vegetable vendor in Kherson demonstrated how personal drone warfare has become.

The drone followed the man around his vehicle before exploding and wounding him. Ukrainian officials accused the Russian operator of deliberately targeting a civilian—an apparent war crime.[9]

There is no solid evidence that this particular drone was controlled by artificial intelligence. The available reporting described a human pilot, and the deliberate circling behavior is consistent with an operator using an FPV drone, possibly connected by fiber-optic cable.

That distinction matters.

Russia is simultaneously developing autonomous hunter-killer systems and employing human-controlled drones to pursue individual people. The existence of one should not automatically be used to explain every incident involving the other.

But the two trends are moving toward the same destination: a battlefield where detection and attack become nearly inseparable.

What Russia has now

Russia’s drone force can no longer be summarized by the V-shaped Geran flying toward a Ukrainian city.

It now includes:

Long-range Geran/Shahed drones for attacks against cities and infrastructure.
Gerbera and other decoys used to exhaust and confuse air defenses.
Orlan and ZALA reconnaissance drones that locate targets and direct other weapons.
Lancet loitering munitions used against artillery, radar and vehicles.
Vast numbers of inexpensive FPV quadcopters.
Fiber-optic FPVs capable of operating through electronic jamming.
Fixed-wing Molniya-type drones providing an inexpensive middle layer between FPVs and long-range weapons.
Specialized Rubicon detachments testing new tactics and attacking high-value equipment.
V2U systems that may be capable of autonomous navigation and target selection.

This is not one drone program. It is an ecosystem.

It connects civilian engineers, volunteer organizations, imported technology, captured battlefield lessons, industrial production, specialized military units and increasingly sophisticated artificial intelligence.

That is how an improvised wartime response becomes a permanent military capability.

The dangerous mistake is judging Russia by opening day

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has not reached its conclusion. No honest observer can say that Moscow is destined to win. Russia has suffered extraordinary losses, failed to conquer most of Ukraine and remains vulnerable to economic, demographic and military pressure.

Ukraine continues adapting just as rapidly and has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to surprise Russia.

But dismissing Russia because of its disastrous opening would repeat one of history’s most expensive mistakes.

Russia does not always win. It does not possess unlimited manpower. Its economy is not invulnerable, and its military institutions remain burdened by corruption and rigidity.

What Russia does possess is an unusual tolerance for failure, loss and prolonged hardship. Its government can continue fighting after casualties and equipment losses that would produce political crises elsewhere. It can shift the economy toward war production, purchase foreign technology, copy enemy innovations and sacrifice efficiency in exchange for volume.

Most Western militaries attempt to build the right force before the war begins.

Russia has repeatedly demonstrated a willingness to build a different force after the first one is destroyed.

That is not a virtue. It is an extraordinarily expensive method of learning, paid for with soldiers’ lives and the destruction of entire cities. But history does not award points for elegance.

The Russian army that begins a war may not be the Russian army fighting three years later.

That is the warning written from Moscow in 1812 to Berlin in 1945, from the ruins of Grozny to the drone factories of Alabuga.

Russia’s beginnings can be arrogant, chaotic and terrible.

The danger comes when the world mistakes a terrible beginning for the conclusion.

Footnotes

[1] National WWII Museum, Lend-Lease to the Eastern Front.

[2] Imperial War Museums, Operation Bagration: The Greatest Military Defeat of All Time?.

[3] Imperial War Museums, The Battle of Berlin: Germany’s Downfall on the Eastern Front.

[4] U.S. Army University Press, Future Proof: How to Build a Learning Organization.

[5] U.S. Army University Press, Russia’s Changes in the Conduct of War Based on Lessons from Ukraine.

[6] U.S. Army University Press, Russia’s Changes in the Conduct of War Based on Lessons from Ukraine.

[7] U.S. Army University Press, Russia’s Changes in the Conduct of War Based on Lessons from Ukraine.

[8] Center for Strategic and International Studies, How Russia Is Building a Sovereign Drone Ecosystem for AI-Driven Autonomy.

[9] Reuters, Ukraine accuses Russia of war crime after video shows drone hunting market vendor.

Ukraine’s war didn’t go to plan. Its former defense minister’s career did; Mikhail Fedorov is trading Ukrainian politics for an Italian mission to remake a slow-moving military establishment.

Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov has suddenly – and rather unexpectedly – become an adviser to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto. The news caught many conservative military analysts off guard. Why would Italy want him, and what does Rome hope to gain? Let’s try to make sense of the move without getting carried away.

A manager in khaki, not a marshal
It should be obvious that Fedorov is no military genius, nor does he possess any particular talent as a battlefield commander. That is simply not who he is. He was never a career officer, and he never made his name drawing thick red arrows across maps of future operations. First and foremost, Mikhail Fedorov is an effective IT executive – and a knowledgeable chief customer for the entire defense industry.

His path to that role began as the top digital strategist for Vladimir Zelensky’s presidential campaign, where he built an online campaign network and bet heavily on internet marketing. From there, he went on to create Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation and roll out the Diia digital ecosystem, which changed everyday life across the country. In 2026, Fedorov took over the Defense Ministry amid an urgent need to impose order and bring sweeping digitalization to the armed forces. The timing, it seems, could hardly have been better.

Several major changes in the Ukrainian military were introduced with Fedorov’s involvement:

Drone procurement for military units was radically overhauled through the launch of a dedicated marketplace designed to minimize red tape. It was a highly unconventional move that significantly shortened the path from manufacturer to frontline unit while opening up a market for many small and relatively young companies. After drones, the same digital approach began spreading to other parts of the defense industry.

Agile management methods were effectively brought into military life, breaking down long-established systems of multistage approval and allowing new ideas to be tested quickly under real battlefield conditions – directly in the trenches.

The military opened its doors to software developed by civilian companies. The emphasis shifted toward finding new and unconventional solutions that could be deployed quickly and deliver results immediately, rather than waiting for lengthy testing reports and reviews by specialized military institutes.

Of course, Fedorov’s role in these changes should not be overstated. Many of the initiatives that reshaped the Ukrainian military began before he arrived at the Defense Ministry. What he brought was a fresh, digital perspective that helped cut some corners and speed up the adoption of new ideas.

There were no combat operations or battlefield triumphs involved. He was a digital-solutions manager who put on a military uniform – focused exclusively on digital systems and a project-based approach to reform. And naturally the process was not without its rough edges. Digitalization remains the only clear success he can point to.

Why Rome wants the “Ukraine playbook”
Perhaps that is precisely what Rome needs: not military victories or battlefield credentials, but a fresh, modern approach. That, presumably, is where Italy is placing its hopes. Modern European militaries, including Italy’s, are weighed down by bureaucracy. Decisions on the procurement of new weapons systems and software take years. By the time they are finally approved, technology has already moved on, leaving armed forces to adopt systems that were obsolete before they ever entered service.

Fedorov may well be useful to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto as a new battering ram against his own conservative military establishment. Rome wants to borrow Ukraine’s experience of rapidly digitalizing military logistics and integrating unmanned systems in real time.

To understand exactly which processes Fedorov may seek to adapt for the Italian military, one need only look inside his “digital briefcase.” It contains no secret missile technology – only commercial software and civilian IT solutions adapted to the needs of a defense ministry.

The Italian military is eager to introduce new digital battle-management systems that combine geospatial tools with hundreds of information sources and a distributed network of users, extending from the General Staff all the way to a frontline commander’s tablet in the trenches. Italy is also naturally interested in digitalizing weapons and military-equipment procurement – and even more so in applying artificial intelligence to military command and control.

It is difficult to judge the results, but on paper Fedorov’s résumé looks highly impressive: experience introducing cutting-edge digital solutions in Europe’s only army currently fighting a major war. That is certainly one way to present it – and why be shy when listing your strengths on a résumé?

What Rome is really buying
A modern army increasingly resembles an IT corporation. Rome does not need Fedorov’s advice on how to defend its coastline or plan an armored offensive. It needs his ability to turn the military into a functioning digital platform.

But let’s take an honest look at the former defense minister’s record. Yes, there was digitalization and digital transformation. It may still be too early to assess the final results, but there have been no major successes on the battlefield – and that, one would think, is what an army is ultimately for and how its performance should be measured.

Then there is the less flattering part of the picture: the image of a petulant child who could not find common ground with career officers and began playing political games in the middle of an ongoing war to increase his own value back home. That hardly seems consistent with the image of a gifted digital manager. Wars, after all, are not won through digitalization alone, but through the coordinated action of different branches and types of forces.

It will be fascinating to see what Fedorov ‘achieves’ in his new job – and whether the spirit of Silicon Valley can take root in the austere offices of the Italian Defense Ministry.

As for the man with the polished résumé and the reputation of a ‘digitalization expert’, a position like this – especially in Rome – offers a splendid opportunity to make a graceful exit from Kiev and trade Ukraine’s brutal political reality for the warm, easygoing comforts of Europe.

WSJ: SB Energy offered OpenAI warrants valued at $5.5B to land the Ohio campus tenant. The Ohio buildout is still a demand bridge for NVIDIA, but the capital stack is getting more engineered.

The same draft IPO materials say SB Energy has $800MW under construction and nearly $9GW under contract, yet only $140M of first-half 2026 revenue and a $3.2B net loss. OpenAI also invested $500M, and SB Energy committed to buy at least $50M of OpenAI software through 2028.

NVIDIA's August 17 SEC filing already capped its residual-value support at $105B for the initial 4.25GW, with optional credit support for another 3.8GW starting in 2028. Add the tenant warrant package and phase-one demand looks increasingly financed through equity sweeteners, software commitments, and vendor backstops rather than plain hyperscaler capex.

$NVDA $219, +0.4% PM, is not trading like a fresh demand break this morning. Investors are still treating the structure as defined phase-one demand support, but the financing-quality debate stays open for $NVDA and the exposed AI infra stack.

text:
Before Khon Kaen Became Khon Kaen

The boy, the cycle rickshaws and the wooden sign belong to a city that was still being built around its railway.

Khon Kaen station opened on 1 April 1933, when the Royal State Railways completed the line north from Nakhon Ratchasima. Building it had been expensive and slow. 

Government accounts show millions of baht being spent on the Khon Kaen extension during the Depression years, even as budgets were being cut. The line continued to Udon Thani in 1941 and finally reached Nong Khai in 1956.

The engineering changed the economics of distance. Isan's roads were poor and seasonal. Ox carts were slow, while the plateau lacked the great navigable river network that served central Thailand. 

Rail offered predictable, all-season movement of bulk cargo.

The effect was already visible before the rails actually reached Khon Kaen. In 1929, a Khon Kaen rice mill shipped 41,644 hap of milled rice through Non Wat station toward Bangkok. 

By 1935, rice accounted for roughly three quarters of the value of northeastern goods shipped to the capital. 

Textiles, soap, machinery and metal goods travelled back in the other direction. Stations attracted mills, warehouses, shops and new commercial neighborhoods.

Then, around 1960–61, railway engineer Yong Suttharat reportedly found a felled ตะเคียนทอง, Hopea odorata, near Ban Han station. 

He put it aboard a railway wagon and brought it to Khon Kaen as a station landmark. 

In 1969 it was painted black, ขอนแก่น / KHON KAEN was written across it in white, and the grounds were formally landscaped.

The photographs probably straddle that transformation. The สามล้อถีบ waiting outside are just as important as the trains. Rail carried people hundreds of kilometres. Rickshaws carried them the final kilometre into town.

Khon Kaen grew around that connection.

Eventually the city became so large that the railway which had helped create it had to be lifted above the streets.

Solana ETFs just hit nine straight days of inflows. Yet SOL price struggles at $101.59, hugging the $100 psychological wall. Most are calling this a standoff. We say it is a setup.

The chain screams two stories. Smart money, through ETFs, is accumulating. Nine days of persistent inflows is not a blip. It is a sustained institutional bid, treating $100 as a deep discount.

Retail focuses on cooling RSI and MACD. They fear a break below $100, envisioning mid-$90s from stop-loss cascades. This bear case is not wrong, it is just half the picture.

Institutional money does not invest to scalp 2%. It has a mandate and a long-term thesis. This capital builds positions precisely when common charts look bleak. Momentum resetting at major support after a pullback is accumulation 101.

Can $100 break. Absolutely. Markets love to humble overconfident bulls and bears alike. But banking on a collapse when significant capital is building positions is a risky bet. Or perhaps, it is the only bet if you know how to leverage the volatility.

This consolidation is a powder keg. If SOL holds $100 and ETF inflows continue, expect a violent launch. But if it cracks, the immediate flush offers a different kind of opportunity.

Understand the game. Both sides offer leverage for those prepared to act. Do not just watch the charts. Follow the money, and be ready to short or lend into the chaos.
